claims.claim: When you believe God is calling you, you should follow even if your family begs you not to.

stances.summary: When my father begged me, for his grey hairs and for my baby, to give up the faith, I refused. I grieved for him, but I could not be anything other than a Christian.
stances.quote: 'Spare the grey hairs of your father, spare the infancy of your boy, offer sacrifice for the well-being of the emperors.' And I replied, 'I will not do so.'
stances.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: Parce, inquit, canis patris tui, parce infantiae pueri. fac sacrum pro salute imperatorum. 4. et ego respondi: Non facio. (Latin Library text of the Passio, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/perp.html)
stances.work: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (the prison diary written in her own hand)
stances.location: ANF chapter 2.2 on New Advent (= sections 6.3-4 in modern numbering; the father's pleading is at modern 3, 5 and 6)
stances.context: Carthage, 203. Perpetua, 22, a nursing mother and a catechumen, writes this part herself. Her father, the only one of her family who would not rejoice in her martyrdom, pleads with her three times: he throws himself at her feet, kisses her hands, calls her "Lady", then appears at the tribunal holding her baby. The words "Spare the grey hairs of your father..." are spoken by the procurator Hilarianus, echoing the father; her answer is the refusal. The family is asking her to deny the faith (to sacrifice), not to turn down a vocation, so this is the plainest case of the claim. Her grief is real: "I grieved over the grey hairs of my father" (2.1). The editor who framed the diary may have had New Prophecy (Montanist) sympathies; Perpetua herself is honoured everywhere as a saint.

stances.summary: Family needs are no excuse for staying in work that compromises with idols. Parents, wives and children must be left behind for God's sake if it comes to that.
stances.quote: Parents, wives, children, will have to be left behind, for God's sake. Do you hesitate about arts, and trades, and about professions likewise, for the sake of children and parents?
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: On Idolatry (De idololatria)
stances.context: He is answering Christian craftsmen who say they cannot give up trades tied to idol-making or pagan cult because they must provide for children and parents. So the family pull here is financial need rather than pleading, and the "call" is to leave a sinful trade. He cites James and John leaving their father and the man told not to go and bury his father. Usually dated about 200, before or near his turn to the New Prophecy (Montanism); the dating is disputed. Tertullian is outside the canonised Fathers because of his later Montanism.

stances.summary: God does not tell us to hate our families. But if a father, child or wife would draw you away from Christ, Christ must win.
stances.quote: Should a brother say the like, should a child, should a wife, should any one whosoever, in preference to all let Christ in you be conqueror. For He contends in your behalf.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (Quis dives salvetur)
stances.context: About 200, Alexandria. Clement softens "hate father and mother" (Luke 14:26): "the God of peace, who also exhorts to love enemies, does not introduce hatred and dissolution from those that are dearest." The break applies only "if one's father, or son, or brother, be godless, and become a hindrance to faith". He then stages a lawsuit: a father says "Follow me, and join with me in wickedness, and obey not the law of Christ", and Christ answers. So he agrees only where the family pulls toward sin or unbelief; he says nothing about leaving home for a special vocation. Hence strength 1.

stances.summary: The love of wife, children and brothers must not hold a Christian back from Christ. Even as a boy I told my imprisoned father not to change his mind for our sake.
stances.quote: he sent to his father an encouraging letter on martyrdom, in which he exhorted him, saying, Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
stances.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 1, 1890 (Eusebius, Church History)
stances.work: Letter to his father Leonides, quoted in Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: Alexandria, about 202. Origen, not yet 17, wanted to join his father in martyrdom; his mother begged him to pity her and finally hid his clothes to keep him home (6.2.4-5), and Eusebius counts that as Providence. Unable to go, Origen, the eldest of seven sons, wrote to his father: "Take heed not to change your mind on our account." Eusebius knew Origen's letters, so this is a near-contemporary record of Origen's words. Decades later (235) his Exhortation to Martyrdom 37 says the same to his patron Ambrose, who had a family (own rendering from the Greek, Koetschau, GCS Origenes Werke 1, 1899, https://archive.org/stream/origeneswerke01orig/origeneswerke01orig_djvu.txt, OCR cleaned): "And you who have a wife and children and brothers and sisters, remember: If anyone comes to Me and does not hate father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, he cannot be My disciple ... So you who have them, hate wife and children and brothers and sisters, that you may help the very ones you hate: by hating them you become a friend of God and gain the freedom to do them good." Greek: "καὶ σὺ μὲν ὁ ἔχων γυναῖκα καὶ τέκνα καὶ ἀδελφοὺς καὶ ἀδελφὰς μέμνησο τοῦ· εἴ τις ἔρχεται πρός με καὶ οὐ μισεῖ τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ τὰ τέκνα καὶ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ τὰς ἀδελφάς, οὐ δύναταί μου μαθητὴς εἶναι ... οὕτως γυναῖκα καὶ τέκνα καὶ ἀδελφοὺς καὶ ἀδελφὰς μίσησον ὁ ἔχων ταῦτα, ἵν᾿ ὠφελήσῃς τοὺς μισουμένους δι᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ μεμισηκέναι παρρησίαν ἀναλαμβάνων πρὸς τὸ εὐεργετεῖν αὐτοὺς φίλος γενόμενος θεῷ." The setting is martyrdom, not a monastic vocation. Origen was condemned long after his death (553) on other doctrines; mark as later judged heterodox.

stances.summary: Bought by Christ's blood, we must put nothing ahead of Him, not father or mother, son or daughter.
stances.quote: That, being redeemed and quickened by the blood of Christ, we ought to prefer nothing to Christ
stances.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Exhortation to Martyrdom, addressed to Fortunatus (Ad Fortunatum)
stances.context: Written about 253-257 to prepare Christians for persecution. The quoted line is Cyprian's own heading; under it he lists Matthew 10:37-38 ("He that loves father or mother more than me...") and Deuteronomy 33:9. The pressure in view is to deny Christ under persecution, and the treatise is mostly a chain of Scripture texts, so the stance is clear but brief (strength 1).

stances.summary: When Christ calls, a mother's tears and a father's pleading must not hold you back. Step over them and go; in this case cruelty is the truest love.
stances.quote: should your father prostrate himself on the threshold, trample him under foot and go your way. With dry eyes fly to the standard of the cross. In such cases cruelty is the only true affection.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: licet in limine pater iaceat, per calcatum perge patrem, siccis oculis ad vexillum crucis vola! Pietatis genus est in hac re esse crudelem. (Perseus Digital Library Latin text of Letter 14, https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2008.01.0566%3Aletter%3D14)
stances.work: Letter 14, to Heliodorus
stances.location: Letter 14, section 2 (the objection "Scripture bids us obey our parents" is answered in section 3)
stances.context: Written from the Syrian desert (NPNF dates it 373-374; many now say about 376) to his friend Heliodorus, who had gone home to Aquileia instead of staying in the desert. Section 3 answers the obvious objection: "Scripture, you will argue, bids us obey our parents. Yes, but whoever loves them more than Christ loses his own soul." Heliodorus did not come; he became bishop of Altinum. In 394 (Letter 52.1) Jerome called the letter youthful and "decked out a good deal with the flourishes of the schools", which disowns the style, not the view. In 384 he said of himself that "for the kingdom of heaven's sake I had cut myself off from home, parents, sister, relations" (Letter 22.30), and in 404 he praised Paula for sailing from Rome while little Toxotius stretched out his hands on the shore: "she overcame her love for her children by her love for God" (Letter 108.6). So he held the view all his life.

stances.summary: Parents often resist a daughter who wants to give herself to God, and their pleading is her first battle. If she wins at home, she wins against the world.
stances.quote: And the anxious entreaties of your parents are your first battles. Conquer your affection first, O maiden. If you conquer your home, you conquer the world.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On Virgins (De virginibus)
stances.location: Book 1, section 63 (sections 58-66 cover this; New Advent prints 62-66 under the heading chapter 12)
stances.context: Milan, 377, addressed to his sister Marcellina. He complains of virgins "prevented from going forward by their mothers" and asks: "Are they, then, who are allowed to choose a man not allowed to choose God?" (58). He says parental support is good but it is "more glorious" when a girl chooses on her own (62), that parents "speak against her, but are willing to be overcome" (63), and he tells of a girl who, pressed by her kin to marry, ran to the altar and put her head under it (65-66). His case is a consecrated virgin resisting a marriage her family wants.

stances.summary: Honour your father, but obey God. Love the one who begot you, but put the One who made you first.
stances.quote: A father must be honoured, but God must be obeyed. He that begot us must be loved, but He that created us must be preferred.
stances.translation: R. G. MacMullen, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 6, 1888
stances.work: Sermon on Luke 9:57-62 (the man who asked first to bury his father)
stances.location: Sermon 50 in the NPNF numbering (= Sermon 100 in the Benedictine numbering), section 2
stances.context: He says the man's "dutiful affection made him delay" and that burying a father is a duty God commands, but "it is place, and time, and circumstance" that give way: "Love your parents, but prefer God to them." Letter 243, to Laetus, a novice whose mother was pulling him back, argues the same for a whole letter (no pre-1929 English; own rendering from Goldbacher, CSEL 57, 1911, https://archive.org/stream/CSEL57/CSEL57_djvu.txt, OCR cleaned): "The trumpet of heaven snatches the soldier of Christ to battle, and his mother holds him back" (6: "rapit militem Christi tuba caelestis ad proelium et retinet mater"); yet "keep dutiful love everywhere; let these things have their place where greater things do not call" (7: "serva potius ubique pietatem; habeant haec locum, ubi maiora non vocant"); and, bluntly, "Does she not want to follow? Let her not hinder you ... what difference does it make whether in a wife or in a mother, so long as Eve is guarded against in any woman?" (10: "sed non vult sequi? non impediat ... quid interest, utrum in uxore an in matre, dum tamen Eva in qualibet muliere caveatur?"). One real limit: with a spouse he says the opposite. Letter 262 tells Ecdicia, who took a vow of continence and gave away goods without her husband's agreement, that without his consent "no number of years would have defended you" ("numerus te nullus defendisset annorum"). So he agrees for parents, not for husbands and wives.

stances.summary: Honour your parents in everything else. But when they ask for more than is due and stand in the way of godliness, do not obey them.
stances.quote: for in those things only does he mean us to obey, as many as do not hinder godliness. For indeed it is a sacred duty to render them all other honors: but when they demand more than is due, one ought not to obey.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 10, 1888
stances.work: Homilies on Matthew
stances.context: Antioch, about 390. Earlier (about 379) he wrote three books Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life, the second to a pagan father and the third to a Christian father whose sons were drawn to the monks. Book 3 opens (own rendering from the Greek, Migne PG 47:349, as printed at https://catholiclibrary.org/library/view?docId=Fathers-Synchronized-EN/John_Chrysostom__Adversus_oppugnatores_vitae_monasticae.en.html&chunk.id=00000049): "Come then, let us now teach the believing father too that he must not make war on those who lead his son toward what pleases God" ("φέρε δὴ λοιπὸν καὶ τὸν πιστὸν πατέρα διδάξωμεν, ὅτι τοῖς ἐνάγουσιν αὐτοῦ τὸν υἱὸν πρὸς τὸ τῷ Θεῷ δοκοῦν πολεμεῖν οὐ χρή"). But in his own youth he deferred to his widowed mother. On the Priesthood 1.5-6 (NPNF 1 vol. 9, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/19221.htm) tells how his mother Anthusa took him to her room, sat beside him on the bed where she had given birth to him, and begged, "do not plunge me into a second widowhood ... wait for my death", and how "the continual lamentations of my mother hindered me" from sharing the ascetic life with his friend Basil (not Basil the Great); he tells it without blaming either of them. So his teaching agrees firmly, while his own early choice honoured his mother.

stances.summary: Whoever is seized by the desire to follow Christ cannot let love of parents or relatives hold him back, when that love goes against the Lord's commands.
stances.quote: So he who is seized by the vehement desire of following Christ can no longer care for anything to do with this life. Not for the love of parents or relations, should it be in opposition to the commands of the Lord
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925); in the US public domain (published before 1929)
stances.work: The Longer Rules (Regulae fusius tractatae)
stances.context: The monastic rules of the 360s-370s. The same rule says the one who renounces "will consider his true parents those who in Christ Jesus begat him through the Gospel". Longer Rule 32 keeps monks from visiting relatives; godly relatives are to be cared for by the whole brotherhood, but with relatives "involved in the life of the world" the monks "have nothing in common". Two limits: the Morals (rule 76.1) say "children must honour their parents and obey them in all things in which God's commandment is not hindered", and Longer Rule 15 receives children still under their parents' control only "when they are brought by them in person", before witnesses, so no runaways. His own turn to the ascetic life came through his sister Macrina, inside the family. Strength 1 because of these qualifications.

stances.summary: I had promised to be the support of my aged parents, and I kept that promise even at the cost of the quiet life of prayer I loved most. Honouring my parents came first.
stances.quote: Now, I had specially pledged myself to become the stay of their old age and the support of their weakness, a pledge which, to the best of my power, I have fulfilled, even at the expense of philosophy itself, the most precious of possessions and titles to me
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 2 (In Defence of His Flight to Pontus)
stances.context: "Philosophy" here means the ascetic, contemplative life, which he held to be the highest calling. Written in 362, after his father ordained him against his will and he fled, then came back; he gives his parents' age as one of the two causes of his return and adds that "there is a time to be conquered". Years earlier (Letter 1, to Basil, about 357-358, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3103b.htm) he had broken his promise to join Basil's ascetic retreat: "one law prevailed against another; I mean the law which bids us honour our parents overpowered the law of our friendship and intercourse", and he offered to split his time, arranged "in such a way that my parents will not be grieved". He did go into retreat, at Seleucia, only after both parents had died (374-375). He also treated obeying his father's wish as obeying God, so he would not say family outranks God; he would say God's call does not ask you to abandon parents who need you.

stances.person: Council of Gangra (a synod of bishops, about 340)
stances.summary: Children who desert their parents, especially believing parents, and deny them due honour on the excuse that they put piety first, are condemned.
stances.quote: If, under any pretence of piety, any children shall forsake their parents, particularly [if the parents are] believers, and shall withhold becoming reverence from their parents, on the plea that they honour piety more than them, let them be anathema.
stances.translation: Henry Percival, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 14, 1900
stances.work: Canons of the Synod of Gangra
stances.location: Canon 16 (with Canon 15, the synodal letter and the epilogue)
stances.context: A synod in Paphlagonia (date disputed, usually put about 340) against followers of Eustathius of Sebaste, whose own words do not survive on this; we know them only through the synod that condemned them. Canon 15 condemns the mirror case, parents who abandon their children "under pretence of asceticism". The synodal letter complains that Eustathians led married women to leave their husbands and husbands their wives. The epilogue insists the synod does not reject genuine ascetic life: "we praise the leaving of worldly occupations, [when it is made] with lowliness of mind". These canons entered the Church's canon law. A council, not a single person; include it only if the quiz allows non-person results.

stances.summary: I refused every new husband my parents proposed and gave my life to God. But I would not leave my mother for a moment; I served her and led her into the same life.
stances.quote: With such words repelling those who tried to talk her over, she settled on one safeguard of her good resolution, in a resolve not to be separated from her mother even for a moment
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Life of St. Macrina (SPCK, 1916)
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
stances.location: section headed "Macrina resolves never to leave her mother" (PG 46:964D-966A)
stances.context: Written by her brother Gregory of Nyssa soon after her death (about 380). Her father had betrothed her; when the young man died, she refused the further matches her parents brought, arguing (in indirect speech) "that it was absurd and unlawful not to be faithful to the marriage that had been arranged for her by her father". So she held her course against her parents' plans, but by turning her father's own decision into her reason, and without leaving home. She stayed with her widowed mother, prepared her meals with her own hands, helped her run a large estate, and drew her (and later her brother Basil) into the ascetic life. A calling followed inside the family rather than against it, hence "mixed". Her words come to us reported by her brother, not in her own hand.

stances.summary: A monk who has left home must not let even letters from his father and mother pull his heart back. Leaving them in body means leaving them in thought too.
stances.quote: And it will be of no use to have forsaken them in the body, if one begins to look on them with the heart, and readmits and revives that memory which on renouncing this world every one gave up, as if he were dead.
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Institutes
stances.location: Book 5, chapter 32 ("Of the letters which were burnt without being read")
stances.context: Southern Gaul, about 420, describing the Egyptian desert. The quoted thought belongs to a monk who, after fifteen years, received a packet of letters from his father, mother and friends in Pontus and burned it unopened; Cassian tells it as the act "of a brother who was intent on purity of heart". Conference 24 (written later in the 420s) is about Cassian himself: he and Germanus confess they want to go home to their pious relatives, and Abba Abraham rebukes them with Luke 14:26 and the story of Abba Apollos, who refused to leave his cell to help his own brother pull an ox from a swamp: "Don't you know that I too have been dead to this world for twenty years" (Conference 24.9, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350824.htm). Cassian is venerated East and West, though some of his views on grace were later disputed.

stances.summary: When our old mother wept at our door to see us, we would not open it. If she gives up seeing us here, she will see us in the world to come.
stances.quote: Dost thou wish to see us here, " or wouldst thou see us in that country [beyond the grave]?" She said unto him, "My sons, if I do not see you here I shall " see you there." And the old man said unto her, "If thou wilt "compel thyself not to see us here, thou shalt, in very truth, " see us there."
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (1907), from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.work: The Sayings of the Holy Fathers (Apophthegmata), in Budge's Paradise
stances.location: Budge vol. 2, "Questions and answers on the rule of life of the holy men", no. 5 (pp. 149-150); the same story stands under Poemen in the Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Egypt, fifth century (Poemen died about 450). His brothers were monks with him. Their mother waited for them on the way to church; they turned back and shut their door, and she stood outside weeping: "Peradventure I did not rear you? Peradventure I am not your mother?" Abba Job asked what to do, and Poemen spoke to her through the door. She left saying she would seek to see them only there. The stray quotation marks at line starts are Budge's running quotes as printed in the OCR text; remove them for display. A similar saying in the same volume (no. 241) has Mark, the disciple of Silvanus, come out to his mother with a blackened face and shut eyes so she would not know him.

stances.summary: Love of relatives is one of Satan's pretexts to draw a solitary out of his calling. A saint rightly refused to leave his cell even for his dying brother, rather than honour nature above Christ.
stances.quote: The blessed one, however, was not to be persuaded even at this time, when natural mercy usually is stirred, to transgress the voluntary borders, saying: ,If I go out, my heart will not be pure before God, for I despise visiting spiritual brethren, should I then honour nature above Christ? So his brother died without his having seen him.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923), from the Syriac; in the US public domain (published before 1929)
stances.work: Mystic Treatises (Ascetical Homilies)
stances.location: Wensinck treatise 41, "A letter ... concerning how Satan contrives to divert the zealous from constant solitude under the pretext of the love of relatives", pp. 205-206
stances.context: Late seventh century; Isaac was briefly bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East, then a hermit, and is read as a saint in the Orthodox Church. The letter is to a brother who loves solitude. After the story he concludes that no one should treat "the weakness of feelings" as a valid reason to break solitude. The ",If" is the OCR of the printed opening quotation mark. This is advice for a hermit's vocation: Isaac is otherwise famous for praising the merciful heart, so his point is not that family love is bad but that it must not undo a calling.

stances.summary: Christ now claims my heart, my words and my time. Do not call me ungrateful to you, my father in all but blood; a Christian cannot lack true love.
stances.quote: To Him given up, whether waiting or serving, in Him laying up my all, think me not, I beseech thee, slothful nor wayward, nor charge me with want of filial piety.
stances.translation: H. G. Evelyn-White, Ausonius vol. 2, Loeb Classical Library, 1921 (Paulinus's reply is printed there as Epistle 31)
stances.original: Huic vacantem vel studentem et deditum, in hoc reponentem omnia, ne quaeso segnem neve perversum putes nec crimineris impium. (same Loeb volume; OCR errors corrected)
stances.work: Poem 10 (Carmen 10), reply to Ausonius
stances.context: About 393-394. Ausonius, his old teacher and patron, wrote several hurt letters begging him to come back from Spain to Aquitaine, to poetry and to his old life. Paulinus calls him "patrone, praeceptor, pater" and says he owes him everything, but Christ now "claims both our hearts and lips and time". Ausonius was not a blood relative, so this fits the claim only by analogy (a father figure's plea). Paulinus did not leave his wife: Therasia shared his renunciation, which fits the view of Augustine and Pelagius that a spouse must consent.

stances.summary: Better to grieve your parents than the Lord, who made you and saved you. Do not be moved by the tears of family and friends, or you will weep for ever.
stances.quote: It is good to grieve your parents rather than the Lord. For He both formed us and saved us, while they have often destroyed those they loved and handed them over to punishment. ... Do not pity the tears of parents or friends; otherwise you will weep for ever.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne PG 88, as on Greek Wikisource)
stances.original: Καλὸν λυπῆσαι γονεῖς, καὶ μὴ Κύριον· ὁ μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἔπλασε, καὶ ἔσωσεν· οἱ δὲ πολλάκις οὓς ἠγάπησαν, ἀπόλεσαν, καὶ τῇ κολάσει παρέδωκαν ... Μὴ οἰκτειρήσῃς γονέων ἢ φίλων δάκρυα· εἰ δὲ μὴ, αἰωνίως μέλλεις δακρύειν.
stances.work: The Ladder of Divine Ascent
stances.context: Sinai, first half of the seventh century. No English before 1929 exists; the familiar English is Moore (1959, copyrighted), so this is my own rendering. The same step balances it: "It is not because we hate our own people or places that we withdraw, God forbid! but to flee the harm that comes to us from them" ("Οὐ μισοῦντες ἡμεῖς τοὺς οἰκείους ἑαυτῶν, ἢ τοὺς τόπους ἀναχωροῦμεν, μὴ γένοιτο! ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἡμῖν προσγινομένην βλάβην ἐκφεύγοντες"), and "longing for God has quenched longing for parents" ("πόθος Θεοῦ ἀπέσβεσεν πόθον γονέων"). He warns that relatives promise to do everything you like, only to block your course. Written for monks.

stances.summary: A monk must not be dragged back by worry for his parents or affection for his relatives, or even see them often. Let the dead bury their dead.
stances.quote: Do not be swept away by cares for your parents or by affection for your relatives. Decline even frequent meetings with them, lest they rob you of the stillness in your cell and draw you into their own troubles. "Let the dead," says the Lord, "bury their own dead; but you, come, follow Me."
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne PG 40:1257)
stances.original: Γονικαῖς μερίμναις ἢ συγγενικαῖς φιλίαις μὴ συναπαχθῇς· ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ πρὸς τούτους αὐτοὺς συνεχεῖς συντυχίας παραιτοῦ, μήποτέ σε ἀποσυλήσωσι τῆς ἐν τῷ κελλίῳ ἡσυχίας, καὶ περὶ τὰς ἑαυτῶν περιστάσεις ἀγάγωσιν. «Ἄφες,» φησὶν ὁ Κύριος, «τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς· σὺ δὲ δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι.»
stances.work: Foundations of the Monastic Life (Rerum monachalium rationes)
stances.context: Egypt (Nitria and Kellia), 380s-390s, advice to a monk seeking stillness; the next chapter tells him to "love exile" from his homeland. The page quoted shows Migne's Greek beside a machine English; only the Greek was used. The only modern English (Sinkewicz, 2003) is copyrighted. Evagrius was condemned with Origenist teachings at the council of 553; mark as later judged heterodox.

stances.summary: Love your kin, but when they stand in your way to God, refuse to know them. Not listening to a relative who urges you wrong is itself a kind of love.
stances.quote: We should love those joined to us by kinship of the flesh, whom we know as our neighbours; but those we suffer as adversaries on the way of God we should refuse to know, by hating and fleeing them. For a man of fleshly mind is loved, as it were, through hatred, when he urges wrong on us and is not heard.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne PL 76)
stances.original: ut eos qui nobis carnis cognatione coniuncti sunt, et quos proximos novimus, diligamus, et quos adversarios in via Dei patimur odiendo et fugiendo nesciamus. Quasi enim per odium diligitur qui carnaliter sapiens, dum prava nobis ingerit, non auditur. (PL 76 OCR, corrected)
stances.work: Forty Homilies on the Gospels (Homiliae in Evangelia)
stances.context: Preached in Rome about 591-593. The same homily says that whoever longs for eternal things must, in God's cause, stand "outside father, outside mother, outside wife, outside children, outside kin, outside himself" ("extra patrem, extra matrem, extra uxorem, extra filios, extra cognatos, extra semetipsum"), and then balances it: "Neighbours must be loved, and charity spent on all, both kin and strangers; yet for the sake of that same charity we must not be turned from the love of God" ("Amandi ergo sunt proximi, impendenda est charitas omnibus et propinquis et extraneis, nec tamen pro eadem charitate a Dei amore flectendum"). The only modern English (Hurst, 1990) is copyrighted, so this is my own rendering.

stances.summary: A wife should not take up a vow to God that her husband has not agreed to. What belongs to two cannot be given away by one.
stances.quote: I have also learned something that troubles and stings me not a little: that you began to keep this great good without your husband's consent and agreement, though the apostle's authority wholly forbids it. ... It is dangerous to promise what is still in another's power, and I do not know how welcome a gift is when one person offers what belongs to two.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Hilberg, CSEL 56)
stances.original: sed illud quoque simul didici, quod me non mediocriter angit ac stimulat, te videlicet tantum hoc bonum absque consensu et pacto viri servare coepisse, cum huic apostolica omnino interdicat auctoritas ... sed periculose promittitur, quod adhuc in alterius potestate est, et nescio, quam sit grata donatio, si unus offerat rem duorum. (CSEL 56 OCR, corrected)
stances.work: Letter to Celantia (Ad Celantiam), transmitted as Jerome's Letter 148
stances.context: Early fifth century, to a married Roman lady who had taken a vow of continence on her own. The letter circulated under Jerome's name but is now generally assigned to Pelagius. He does not tell her to break the vow; he calls it a double danger and tells her to honour her husband and win him to it. This concerns a spouse only; no statement of his about parents was found. Augustine's Letter 262 to Ecdicia takes the same line. Pelagius was condemned in 418 and at Ephesus in 431; mark as heterodox.

splits_fathers: Most early Christians agree, and on one version of the question they agree almost to a man: when family pressure means denying Christ or sinning, you follow Christ (Perpetua, Origen, Clement, Cyprian, Tertullian, Chrysostom, Augustine). The real split comes when the call is to a religious vocation (desert, monastery, virginity) and the family simply loves or needs you. Firmly for going anyway: Jerome, Ambrose, Basil's Longer Rules, Chrysostom's Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life, Augustine's Letter 243, Cassian, Poemen, Evagrius, Isaac, Climacus and Gregory the Great. Real voices on the other side: Gregory of Nazianzus (honouring his parents overruled the ascetic life he loved), the Council of Gangra (condemns children who leave believing parents on the plea of piety), and Macrina (followed her call without ever leaving her mother). Chrysostom himself put off his own call for his widowed mother. With a spouse the Fathers flip: Augustine (Letter 262) and Pelagius (Ad Celantiam) both say a vow made without the partner's consent is wrong.
splits_people_today: Genuinely split, which makes it useful. Many committed Christians, especially evangelicals raised on missionary stories and converts from other faiths, would agree and cite "hate father and mother" and "let the dead bury their dead". Many others would disagree or hesitate: people from family-centred cultures (much of Asia, Africa, Latin America, and many Catholic and Orthodox homes), anyone wary of groups that use "God told me" to cut people off from family (the cult worry), and Christians who think God does not call anyone to break the command to honour parents. Non-religious people tend to reject the "God is calling you" frame but often accept a secular version (follow your own path even if your parents object). Answers shift with details: adult or teenager, converting or entering a monastery or moving abroad, believing or unbelieving parents. I found no survey that measures this directly.

misattributions.line: Letter to Celantia (Ad Celantiam), printed as Jerome's Letter 148
misattributions.truth: Transmitted among Jerome's letters (the CSEL 56 manuscript heading still reads "Hieronymus ad Celantiam"), but now generally assigned to Pelagius. Quote it as Pelagius, not Jerome.

misattributions.line: The English text of Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life at catholiclibrary.org
misattributions.attributed_to: John Chrysostom (as if a published translation)
misattributions.truth: The page marks its English as machine translation (data-ensrc="MT"). It is not a published translation and must not be quoted as Chrysostom's words in English. The Greek on the same page (Migne PG 47) is reliable; the only published English is Hunter (1988, copyrighted).

misattributions.line: "Though your father lie across the threshold, trample him"
misattributions.truth: Genuine in content but loose wording. The public-domain NPNF reads "should your father prostrate himself on the threshold, trample him under foot and go your way"; the Latin is "licet in limine pater iaceat, per calcatum perge patrem". Quote the NPNF wording.

notes: For the quiz writer. (1) The claim hides two questions. If the family asks you to deny the faith, nearly every Father agrees, so an item framed that way will not separate people or Fathers. If the family begs you not to take up a vocation, the Fathers divide, so frame the statement around a calling such as ministry, mission or a religious life, not apostasy. (2) If the statement names a husband or wife, Augustine and Pelagius move to disagree, and Paulinus took his wife with him; keep the item about parents to keep the sides clean. (3) Strong "farthest" pairs: Jerome ("trample him under foot and go your way") against Gregory of Nazianzus ("the law which bids us honour our parents overpowered"); Climacus ("better to grieve your parents than the Lord") against Gangra canon 16; Perpetua against Chrysostom's mother scene in On the Priesthood 1.5. (4) Numbering traps: New Advent's ANF Perpetua has six chapters, so the father scenes are ANF 1.2, 2.1-2 and 3.1 (modern 3, 5, 6, 9); New Advent prints Ambrose On Virgins 1.62-66 under "chapter 12"; Augustine's Sermon 50 on New Advent is Sermon 100 in the Benedictine numbering. (5) Voices found without quotable words of their own, so no stance: Martin of Tours (Sulpicius, Life of Martin 2: at ten he went to church "against the wish of his parents", https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm); Melania the Younger (only Rampolla's 1908 narrative found: married against her will at 13, obeyed outwardly, renounced with her husband after her father died); Paula (Jerome's narration, Letter 108.6); Benedict (Gregory's Dialogues 2.1, he slipped away from his nurse); Theodore of Tabennesi and Pachomius (Pachomian Lives, modern English only); Thecla (the Acts of Paul and Thecla are legend, not a record); Eustathius of Sebaste (known only through Gangra). Nothing on this question was found for Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Novatian, Lactantius, Athanasius, Ephrem, Hilary, Antony, Amma Syncletica, Moses the Black, Arsenius (his "I died before him" concerns a relative's inheritance, not a plea) or Boethius. (6) Own renderings (Climacus, Evagrius, Gregory the Great, Pelagius, and the extra lines in the Origen, Augustine and Chrysostom contexts) are mine; their Latin and Greek were read in the sources named, from OCR where noted, and lightly corrected. (7) Several quotations come from archive.org OCR text files (Basil, Poemen, Isaac, Paulinus); they match that text exactly, including Budge's running quotation marks and Wensinck's low opening quote, which should be cleaned for display.
